newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolia shuts biggest commercial bank over losses.
newsitem.headline: Mongolia shuts biggest commercial bank over losses.

text.p: Mongolia's central bank has shut down two commercial banks -- one of them the nation's biggest -- to try to stem huge losses from bad debts and boost reforms of the troubled financial sector, officials said.

Hundreds of police were standing guard over documents as investigators picked through the financial ruins of the People's Bank and the Insurance Bank after the central bank cancelled their licences, officials said late on Monday.

"These two banks had been losing one billion tugriks ($1.43 million) a month," parliamentary speaker R. Gonchigdorj told Mongolian Radio after the announcement that the two institutions had been closed last Friday.
"There was absolutely no hope of them overcoming their financial difficulties on their own," Gonchigdorj said.

The central bank said the closures were part of financial reforms promised by Mongolia's new democratic coalition government, which has vowed to bring free-market discipline to the debt-ridden and inefficient banking sector.
Officials promised to make sure private depositors at the two commercial banks received their money back, but said it was too early to estimate losses to other investors and the state.
Huge bad debts and losses had made salvaging the banks impossible, J. Unenbat, governor of the Bank of Mongolia, the central bank, told a news conference at the weekend.
"These banks ended up making big losses, with over 60 percent of their loans non-paying," Unenbat said.
Central bank officials said they closed down the People's Bank, which is 50 percent state-owned, after it lost an estimated 17.4 billion tugriks.
The central bank shut down the Daatgal Bank, or Insurance Bank, a medium-sized commercial bank, after it lost an estimated 5.9 billion tugriks, Unenbat said.

The People's Bank had total debts of 22.5 billion tugriks at the end of October, while the Daatgal Bank's debts had climbed to 4.5 billion tugriks, official figures from the State Statistical Centre showed.

More than 300 policemen guarded 165 branches of the two banks over the weekend as investigators worked their way through piles of documents to try to clarify the financial situation. Telephone lines to the banks were cut.
Officials said the government would open two new state-run banks to take over from the bankrupt institutions.

Individual accounts would be transferred to the Savings Bank, while company accounts would be moved to the Sergeen Bosgolt Bank. The new institutions would at first use the premises of the People's Bank and the Insurance Bank, they said.
The government last Friday created a new agency to pursue companies and individuals with unpaid debts to the two banks.
Gonchigdorj said the government would continue its campaign to clean up the banking system in this largely nomadic north Asian nation.

"In the future, we will increase the control and investigations in all commercial banks," he said. "We are going to create a system where all banks carry out their activities in the way they are supposed to." ($1 = 690 tugriks)
